name: Jamal Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead hand on the formwork crew for Northgate Build. We're doing a six-storey block of flats by the old bus depot. Formwork is the carpentry nobody sees: we build the plywood and timber moulds, the concrete gets poured in, and then we strip it all out and move up a floor. I'm on site at seven. Before the crew gets in, I've already run the day's drawings through an app on my tablet that marks up where every prop and panel goes. Some mornings I fly my drone round the floor to send progress photos to the office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a pour day. Everything has to be right, because if a mould fails you've got tonnes of wet concrete on the floor and everyone's shouting. When it holds and the faces come out clean, that's the best feeling on site. What wears me out is the pay for the responsibility. I'm the one who signs off that the forms are safe, and I earn less than the crane driver. There aren't many other firms doing this kind of work round here, so I can't push too hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and I'll keep using it. I'd probably post a video of my drawing app saving me an hour and say, this is what AI actually does on a site, no robots taking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I stay a bit ahead of the others, because I'm the one who uses the tools. Doesn't change my pay though. That's the boring truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the apps every day and maybe build the drone side up. I already do the odd weekend job filming houses for an estate agent, maybe two a month. I'd push that to four if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty relaxed, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drone. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought it second-hand last year and did the licence online, cost me nearly two months of savings in one go. The office laughed at first. Now the site manager asks for my photos every Friday. I wish they'd pay for the batteries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, where's your money at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. Two or three weeks in the bank. I send some to my parents every month, and the drone ate the rest. Nothing changing means I'd slowly build it back up with the weekend filming.

S0.say: I'd say it's a decent tool and I'll keep using it. I'd post a video of my drawing app saving an hour and say that's what AI really does on a site.
S0.think: It means I stay a bit ahead because I'm the one who uses the tools. It doesn't change my pay, though, which is the boring truth.
S0.do: Keeps using AI drawing apps daily on site. Grows his weekend drone filming for an estate agent from about two jobs a month to four to rebuild his savings.
S0.quote: The office laughed at first. Now the site manager asks for my photos every Friday.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal is a confident early adopter who has already spent his savings on kit, a drone and licence, that now earns him a side income. He is unbothered by AI fizzling out. His money is thin partly because he supports his parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn it or get left behind, that's just how it is. Not in a nasty way. I'd show people the tools if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one's good for me. I'm already the guy who sorts the tablet and the drone. When the robots come, someone has to set them up, and I'd want that to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Northgate and say put me on every new machine first. I'd look for any robot operator or site technology course and do it in the first year, even if I paid myself. And I'd watch the bigger firms, because they'll bring the kit in first and pay for people who can run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. Like being early to a new trend for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, who's been doing formwork for thirty years. He's brilliant, but he can't stand screens. If the forms come pre-made from a factory, Pete's knowledge matters less, and that's not fair on him. I'd try to pair up with him so he sees the new stuff isn't scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Northgate if a better offer came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the money was right. I'm loyal, but I'm not loyal to being underpaid. If a bigger firm wanted someone to run their robots, I'd go, even with a longer drive.

S1.say: I'd say learn it or get left behind, not in a nasty way, just how it is. I'd show anyone the tools if they asked.
S1.think: This one's good for me, since I'm already the one who sorts the tablet and drone. When the robots come, someone has to set them up, and I want that to be me.
S1.do: Asks to be first on every new machine at Northgate and takes a robot operator or site technology course in the first year, paying himself if needed. Watches bigger firms and would move for better pay running their kit.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like being early to something new.
S1.quote: I'm loyal, but I'm not loyal to being underpaid.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees steady change as an opening and would move fast. He still thinks about an older colleague who struggles with screens, and would pair up with him. His loyalty to his employer has a clear price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is massive and people need help to get through it, but there's no point pretending we can stop it. I'd tell people to get close to the new tech, not run from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with apps doesn't count for much if the machine does the whole job. My advantage is a year, maybe two. And I've got three weeks of money, so I can't afford to get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go after a job with whichever company is installing the robots, setting them up, fixing them, anything. I'd move to the city if that's where it was. I'd cut back hard, sell the drone if I had to, and tell my parents I'd need to send less for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I think I'd cope, but I'd feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move. Where to, and how would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city, where the big building firms and the robot suppliers are. I'd sleep on my cousin's sofa for a couple of months, he's offered before. The drone money and the last pay would cover the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine, I've got a plan, and I need to cut what I send for a few months. My dad would worry. My mum would ask if I'm eating. I'd tell them the truth but the short version.

S2.say: I'd say this is massive and people need help, but there's no point pretending we can stop it. I'd tell people to get close to the new tech, not run from it.
S2.think: Being good with apps doesn't count for much if the machine does the whole job; my lead is a year or two. With three weeks of money, I can't afford to get it wrong.
S2.do: Goes after a job installing, setting up or fixing robots for the supplier firms, moving to the city and sleeping on his cousin's sofa if needed. Cuts back hard, sells the drone if he must and sends less money to his parents.
S2.feel: Anxious but coping, feeling the clock.
S2.quote: My dad would worry. My mum would ask if I'm eating.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest picture, Jamal moves rather than freezes, and has a plan with names and places. His limit is money, not willingness. Cutting what he sends his parents is the part that clearly bothered him most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if people start now. Get on the courses, get on the kit. I'd post about the courses I was doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is good for me. Enough time to get qualified properly and save a bit, and I'd be one of the first people round here who knows the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a robotics maintenance course in the first year, evenings. Build up the drone side, maybe add 3D scanning of buildings, which people pay good money for. And I'd save every bit of the side money, aiming for three months in the bank by year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of business would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scanning and surveying sites with a drone and a laser scanner, maybe setting up and checking robots for small builders who can't afford their own tech person. A one-man band at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got almost no savings. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, that's why I'd keep the day job while I build it. I'm not going to quit Northgate with three weeks in the bank. That would be stupid, and I'm not stupid.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if people start now. Get on the courses and the kit, and I'd post about the courses I was doing.
S3.think: Five years is good for me: enough time to qualify properly and save, and I'd be one of the first round here who knows the machines.
S3.do: Takes an evening robotics maintenance course in the first year. Builds his drone work into 3D building scanning, saving all side income towards three months of cushion by year two while keeping his day job.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more interested than scared.
S3.quote: I'm not going to quit Northgate with three weeks in the bank.
S3.fieldNote: Jamal is adaptive but careful about cash: he would build a side business without leaving his job. Five years fits his style of moving early. He sees a niche in serving small builders who can't afford their own technology staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best of the three, there's time to do it properly. I'd tell people to start learning now while it's still a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite good about it. Ten years is enough to build a small business around the new stuff before it fully arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, but steadier. Keep at Northgate a few years, do the courses, build the scanning business slowly. By year three I'd want to buy a proper laser scanner, and by year five I'd hope to go full-time on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a buzz about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is there anything that worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that everyone else catches up. In two years I'd be ahead. In ten, every kid with a phone will know the machines too. So I'd have to keep being early, which is fine, that's my thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned buying a scanner. With what money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings from the drone jobs, and a small loan once I've got a track record. I wouldn't borrow before I had regular clients. A scanner is a lot of money to have sitting in a cupboard.

S4.say: I'd say this is the best of the three, because there's time to do it properly. I'd tell people to start learning while it's still a choice.
S4.think: I'd feel quite good about it. Ten years is enough to build a small business around the new technology before it fully arrives.
S4.do: Stays at Northgate for a few years while doing courses and slowly growing a scanning business. Buys a laser scanner around year three from savings and a small loan once he has regular clients, aiming to go full-time on his own by year five.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a bit of a buzz.
S4.quote: In ten, every kid with a phone will know the machines too.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Jamal's only worry is losing his early lead as others catch up. His plan is staged and cautious about borrowing. He is the clearest example of someone who would rather have time to build than have no competition.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no money to get through the gap, even though I'd know what to do. What would help is cheap or free short courses on the new machines, and some kind of loan or grant for people starting small businesses around them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the older guys. People like me will be all right. Someone like Pete, with thirty years in formwork and no time for screens, he's the one I'd worry about. His knowledge shouldn't just disappear.

headlineQuote: When it holds and the faces come out clean, that's the best feeling on site.
portrait: Jamal is a 27-year-old formwork lead hand on a block of flats, who uses AI drawing apps every day and taught himself to fly a drone for site photos. He shares a house, sends money to his parents and has two or three weeks of savings, much of it spent on the drone. He is calm in the slower pictures, seeing robots as his chance, and only anxious when AGI arrives in two years, when he would move to the city and chase work installing robots. With more time he would build a side business scanning buildings, staying cautious about money and worried mostly for older colleagues like Pete.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because even knowing what to do, he'd have no money to get through the gap.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free short courses on the new machines, and loans or grants for people starting small businesses around them.
